title: Longitudinal effects of ambient artificial intelligence scribe use on documentation burden and financial productivity in primary care: a quasi-experimental study.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To investigate the longitudinal effects of an ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribe use in primary care on outcomes related to documentation time, note writing patterns, and clinician financial productivity. We conducted a quasi-experimental study with an interrupted time-series design to ascertain the effect of AI scribe use on note writing time, time outside of scheduled hours (TOSH), pajama time (5:30PM-7:00aM), note length, note closure <24 h, and work relative value units (wRVU). For each primary care clinician (physician, advanced practice provider), date of initial access was day 0; each measure was calculated for 150 days prior (pre-period) and after (post-period) day zero. Two hundred and twenty clinicians (mean age = 43.7, 70.9% females; 56.4% physicians) from 36 clinics, conducting 314 845 patient encounters were included. Compared to the pre-period, there was 7% decrease in note writing time at day 0 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.93, 95% credible interval [CI] [0.89, 0.98]), increasing to 16% decrease by day 150 (IRR 0.84, 95% CI [0.82, 0.87]). There was no change in pajama time, TOSH, or wRVU at day 0; however, at day 150, there was a 19% decrease in pajama time (0.81, 95% CI [0.73, 0.90]), 13% decrease in TOSH (0.87, 95% CI [0.77, 0.98]), and a 2% increase in wRVU (1.02, 95% CI [1.01, 1.04]). At day 0, there was a 5% increase in note closures (1.05, 95% CI [1.02, 1.08]), with no difference to pre-period levels by day 150. There were no changes in note length at day 0 or day 150. There were persistent changes in AI scribe use measures over time as clinicians situated these tools within their workflows.

title: Evidence Synthesis of the Ethical and Legal Challenges of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Provision of Patient Health Information.
desc: [Healthcare technology letters] Large language model (LLM)-based generative AI offers the promise of responsive health information for patients and carers but presents ethical and legal challenges when used outside clinical oversight. This review maps these considerations for patients accessing information on long-term conditions in non-clinical settings. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, EMBASE, and Web of Science) between April and May 2025. The review synthesises 24 cross-sectional studies regarding patient-facing LLMs, excluding clinician-support tools. Results indicate that LLMs perform well on general topics but struggle with specialised information, often generating complex responses with unreliable citations. Ethical concerns highlight inaccuracy, insufficient empathy, and the potential exacerbation of health inequalities, while analyses of legal challenges focus mainly on liability and consent. We conclude that current technical limitations and regulatory gaps regarding device classification and safety obligations could pose risks to patients. Consequently, stakeholders must establish clear accountability frameworks, and LLMs should currently function only as supplementary tools rather than replacements for expert clinical advice. Further research into the use of agent-based LLM architectures, where specialised LLM agents collaborate to verify information, reason symbolically, and interface with patient health records under strict data governance, may provide the solution to the current limitations of LLMs.

title: CRUX: Clinical-Text Anchoring for Cross-Institutional CT-Pathology Fusion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
desc: Accurate prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) benefits from integrating computed tomography (CT) and histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), which capture complementary macroscopic and microscopic disease characteristics. Fusing these modalities is difficult: their features come from different pretrained foundation-model encoders and lack spatial correspondence, and both are sensitive to institution-specific acquisition and staining, causing multimodal models to overfit site-specific artifacts and generalize poorly. We present CRUX (CRoss-modal Unification via teXt anchoring), a fusion framework that uses clinical text---encoded by a biomedical language model---as an institution-invariant semantic anchor. Because clinical variables follow standardized classification systems, their embeddings occupy a representation space that is consistent across institutions, providing a stable reference frame for aligning heterogeneous imaging features. CRUX introduces a text-mediated cross-modal bridge in which CT- and pathology-derived text-query summaries exchange information within a compact text semantic space through a learnable hub token, avoiding direct image-space cross-attention that would propagate domain-specific artifacts. We evaluate on 2,157 NSCLC patients from five hospitals, holding out one hospital (N=446) entirely for external validation. CRUX attains an external concordance index (C-index) of 0.761, the highest among all unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal configurations. Notably, direct CT-WSI fusion degrades under distribution shift, whereas text anchoring restores and improves cross-institutional generalization. These results indicate that language-model-encoded clinical text is an effective structured prior for robust, generalizable multimodal cancer prognosis.

title: Determining cellular phylogeny and migration at high resolution in spatial genomics
desc: Cellular migration and tumor evolution are central to tissue homeostasis and cancer biology. Rapid advances in spatial genomics have raised the possibility of using somatic mutations to track these processes in situ in human tissues. However, frequent data dropouts in spatial genomics measurements make this challenging to implement. Here, we present StarTrak (SpaTial Analysis for lineage ReconsTRuction with somatic vAriant calling and tracKing), a framework for somatic variant calling and lineage reconstruction at single-pixel spatial resolution. StarTrak employs a neural network framework to integrate mutational evidence (from both nuclear and mitochondrial reads), spatial proximity, histological images, and transcriptomic states to identify spatially informative patterns of mutations. It performs robustly across tissue types and spatial-omics platforms (being particularly successful with spatial ATAC-seq). Applying StarTrak to tumor sections, we infer the migration of mutated tumor cells into adjacent non-malignant tissues and reconstruct distinct lineage trees associated with different spatial regions. Notably, we identify tumor regions with nearly identical transcriptomic states but distinct mutational profiles. Moreover, for skin sections, StarTrak identifies sunlight-associated mutations in non-malignant epidermis and evidence suggesting the migration of these mutant surface cells into deeper skin layers. Overall, by integrating mutation calling with spatial context, StarTrak enables the inference of spatially resolved cellular migration and cellular phylogeny.

Do People Still Matter? Healthcare in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
source: PubMed · American journal of lifestyle medicine
desc: [American journal of lifestyle medicine] Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent in healthcare. Unlike previous technologies, AI has the capability to perform tasks previously considered uniquely human including synthesizing historical information and data to establish a clinical diagnosis and constructing a treatment plan. AI promises to improve diagnostic accuracy, accelerate drug discovery and development, and enhance access to healthcare. The overall impact that AI will have on the well-being of individuals who provide and receive care, however, is less obvious. This article examines the potential and pitfalls of AI in medicine through the lens of mattering and its importance to human flourishing. Mattering is a psychological construct that encompasses the human needs to be noticed, feel significant, and contribute. It arises from interpersonal interactions and is based on perceptions of our value within our communities and society. Mattering is inherently relational, is a significant contributor to psychological well-being, and may be at risk in the age of AI. The authors describe the foundations of mattering and its relevance to medicine; the potential impacts of AI on mattering in medicine from the clinician, patient, and trainee perspectives; and propose a framework for integrating AI into healthcare such that mattering is preserved for all stakeholders.

title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
desc: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index. For fixed-fraction high-intensity regions, NSNet-D was marginally higher in slice-level recall and balanced accuracy, but the equal-weight patient-level values were nearly identical and the highest Dice values shifted to TransNSNet. These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. TransNSNet also had a substantially smaller parameter footprint than the original next-scale models. These findings indicate promising image-quality trends, but they do not establish statistical superiority or clinical validity; synthesized PET-like images should not be interpreted as substitutes for clinically acquired PET.

title: LigRNA: High-accuracy prediction of RNA-ligand binding sites via dynamic chemical complementarity and language model encoding
desc: RNA-binding small molecules represent a validated therapeutic modality, yet pinpointing their exact RNA binding sites remains critical for mechanistic understanding and drug optimization. Experimental methods, while precise, are costly and low-throughput, necessitating robust computational alternatives. Approaches based on static feature concatenation may overlook input-dependent relationships between RNA residues and ligand functional groups. Here we present LigRNA, a graph neural network framework that predicts RNA-ligand binding sites through joint cross-modal encoding of both molecules. LigRNA integrates structure-guided language model embeddings with physicochemical features-solvent-accessible surface area and secondary structure types, to construct comprehensive RNA representations. Ligands are encoded as attributed molecular graphs via graph attention networks, preserving atom-level chemical topology rather than compressing molecules into fixed fingerprints. A cross-attention mechanism then enables dynamic, ligand-dependent modulation of RNA nucleotide attention, capturing context-specific interaction patterns. Benchmarked on TE9 and TE18 datasets, LigRNA achieves F1 scores of 0.73 and 0.58, improving on GATRsite by 7.4% and 18.4%, respectively. Ablation studies identify the RNA residual encoder as the most consistent contributor across the two benchmarks. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/WillowWang0216/LigRNA.

From inherited susceptibility to tumor state: toward a stage-aware architecture for genomic risk stratification in prostate cancer.
desc: [Frontiers in genetics] Prostate cancer risk is currently represented by two largely separate genomic layers. Germline polygenic scores estimate inherited susceptibility before diagnosis, whereas tumor genomic and transcriptomic classifiers estimate biological aggressiveness and treatment response after tissue acquisition. Artificial intelligence can connect these layers, but simply concatenating high-dimensional features is unlikely to produce transportable clinical tools. This Mini Review examines how biologically informed machine learning, single-cell and spatial atlases, whole-omics response models, and validated tissue classifiers are reshaping prostate cancer risk stratification. We argue that the most useful architecture is a stage-aware system: ancestry-calibrated germline risk first modifies screening intensity; tissue or liquid-biopsy models then resolve tumor state; and longitudinal molecular measurements update risk under treatment. Evidence is strongest for polygenic enrichment of screening populations and for locked transcriptomic classifiers tested in randomized-trial cohorts. By contrast, many multi-omics models remain retrospective, dataset-dependent, and weakly calibrated across ancestry, disease stage, and specimen type. Progress requires explicit clinical decision points, external and prospective validation, uncertainty reporting, ancestry-aware calibration, and comparisons against simpler clinicopathological models. A unified framework should therefore treat artificial intelligence not as a single prognostic score, but as an auditable sequence of genomic updates that links inherited susceptibility to evolving tumor biology.

title: The Model Knows Better: Defending Medical Multi-Agent Systems Against Prompt Injection
desc: Medical multi-agent systems, in which LLM agents discuss a case, are increasingly studied for clinical decision support. Prompt injection, text that an attacker adds to a model's input, can manipulate LLMs into wrong decisions. How it affects these systems, and how to protect them, remains unclear. Across two systems, two model families and three benchmarks, a single injected passage succeeds in up to 61% of cases, and collaboration does not consistently protect against it. Existing defenses help only partly: they miss injections that look like ordinary clinical text. Yet when asked to check the injected text against the patient's findings, a model that followed the injection usually rejects it. We therefore propose a training-free defense that verifies the clinical judgments behind the system's decision. Following clinical practice, it separates the patient's findings from clinical judgments, such as diagnoses, recommendations and instructions, and checks each judgment against the findings alone, so the decision rests only on supported judgments. Our defense outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, lowering attack success on MedQA to 4-7% while maintaining accuracy on cases without an attack, and remains effective with a medical model and against defense-aware and adaptive attacks.

title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
desc: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.

The application progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.
desc: [Frontiers in neurology] Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, where traditional diagnostic methods are constrained by limited sensitivity and restricted clinical utility. This review synthesizes recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in AD diagnostics, focusing on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) across neuroimaging modalities and multi-omics research. AI algorithms can automatically extract subtle microstructural, metabolic, and molecular features, enabling high-precision classification of AD stages, patient stratification, and non-invasive early screening through multimodal data integration. However, translating AI into routine clinical practice still faces critical challenges, including high equipment costs, insufficient model generalizability across real-world cohorts, data class imbalance, and complex cross-platform standardization barriers. Future research should prioritize cost-effective surrogate modeling, robust multi-center validation, dynamic longitudinal integration, and mechanistic interpretability to accelerate the standardized clinical translation of AI-driven AD diagnostics.

title: LGGS: Longitudinal MRI Reconstruction via Guided Group Sparsity
desc: Serial MRI is routinely performed in current clinical practice for disease surveillance and applications such as MR-guided radiotherapy. However, long MRI scan times increase costs and limit patient access, making accelerated image reconstruction of broad clinical importance. Previous scans of the same patient contain image information highly correlated with the current exam, yet existing reconstruction methods rarely exploit this information. Major challenges in the effective use of prior scans include inter-visit misregistration, pathological changes, and image phase variation. In this work, we propose Longitudinal Guided Group Sparsity (LGGS), an interpretable deep-learning framework for longitudinally informed MRI reconstruction derived from classical group sparsity. The prior scan is incorporated into the reconstruction regularizer through learned phase-invariant circulant attention that identifies corresponding features across exams. This formulation provides robustness to local in-plane and through-plane misregistration as well as inter-visit phase variation. Across acceleration rates, LGGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on longitudinal T1-weighted multi-coil brain MRI data, outperforming the evaluated unguided and longitudinally informed reconstruction methods, with substantially fewer learned parameters. We further evaluated the contributions of multiple guide slices and phase-invariant similarity and demonstrated that accelerated prior images can also serve as effective guides with minimal degradation in reconstruction quality.

title: PATHNet: A Thermodynamic Path-Integral-Inspired Neural Network for Protein-Ligand Interaction Prediction
desc: Protein-ligand scoring functions must capture strongly nonlinear, target-dependent binding physics while remaining generalizable beyond their training data, a balance that purely analytic and purely data-driven models each struggle to achieve on their own. We present PATHNet, a physics-informed framework that learns this unknown functional relationship from molecular-mechanics descriptors using a non-monotonic piecewise-linear mapper with a bounded neural-network correction, trained through a variational, least-action-inspired objective and regulated by a renormalization-group-inspired spectral constraint, with model selection performed through multi-start basin optimization. Across seven DUD-E targets, PATHNet achieved the highest mean active inactive/decoy classification accuracy among the methods tested, outperforming three literature baselines representing distinct architectural families. These results support a physics-grounded, variationally constrained approach to neural-network scoring as a practical route toward more interpretable and transferable protein-ligand interaction models.

Toxoplasmosis: Epidemiological Significance, Economic Burden, and Emerging Directions in Drug Discovery and Artificial Intelligence.
desc: [International journal of microbiology] Toxoplasmosis, a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, affects a wide range of warm-blooded hosts and remains most prevalent in tropical regions, with distribution shaped by climate, cultural practices, and environmental conditions. Clinical severity varies across susceptible populations, generating substantial economic burdens through medical costs and agricultural losses. Given this global health impact, a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of the disease is essential. However, significant gaps persist. While diagnostic techniques and epidemiological surveillance have advanced considerably, treatment protocols have remained largely unchanged for decades, revealing a disconnect between diagnostic innovation and therapeutic progress. Moreover, existing literature lacks an integrative synthesis connecting these advances to their broader significance, leaving researchers without a unified framework for understanding where the field stands and where it should go next. To address these gaps, this narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature and institutional reports across major biomedical databases, synthesizing findings descriptively and thematically rather than through statistical meta-analysis. It critically examines toxoplasmosis across several dimensions. It first considers geographical distribution and the cultural, environmental, and economic factors shaping its epidemiology. It then turns to the parasite's biochemical and molecular characteristics, using this foundation to evaluate persistent limitations in treatment and vaccine development, an area where progress has stalled. In response, the review explores emerging alternatives, including plant-based compounds, as avenues beyond conventional pharmacological strategies. Finally, it examines artificial intelligence as an underexplored but promising tool for improving diagnosis and treatment, an area with limited application to toxoplasmosis specifically. By consolidating these threads, this review clarifies not only what is known about toxoplasmosis but also where critical gaps in treatment innovation and integrative understanding continue to hinder effective prevention and control.

title: Alert-List Concordance for Evaluating Imputation Strategies in ICU Sepsis Prediction
desc: Preprocessing is an under-measured reliability risk in clinical prediction: a model can keep a similar AUROC and still change who receives an alert. Imputation quality is commonly evaluated using reconstruction error or aggregate discrimination, neither of which directly measures agreement on which patients are flagged. At a matched alert rate, pipelines with similar aggregate performance can produce different patient lists. This question is especially relevant under the frequent, structured missingness of real ICU records. We therefore introduce alert-list concordance, which asks whether two pipelines identify the same high-risk patients, measured by the Jaccard similarity of their top-k% alert sets with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. On PhysioNet/CinC 2019 (40,336 patients, 71.9% missingness), we compare nine imputation strategies and a native-missingness baseline using a fixed XGBoost configuration, fitted and Platt-calibrated separately for each strategy. After Bonferroni correction, 22 of the 28 reconstruction-method pairs showed no statistically significant difference in patient-level AUROC, yet their alert lists overlap at Jaccard 0.518 to 0.750. Similar aggregate discrimination can therefore accompany different patient selections. ForwardFill is a separate outlier, pairing higher discrimination with the lowest overlap in the matrix, 0.40 to 0.45. The broad pattern holds within each hospital system and under six patient-level aggregation rules. At the row level, eight of ten methods fall within an AUROC range of 0.011. In this row-level pipeline, deep imputers did not outperform mean imputation on discrimination, and the sequential implementations cost 5 to 12 times mean imputation in total pipeline wall-clock time on our hardware.

title: Scalable Enzyme Reaction Retrieval Enables Metagenomic Biocatalyst Discovery
desc: Enzyme catalyzed reactions drive metabolism and enable diverse applications in biotechnology and sustainable synthesis, but assigning catalytic functions to uncharacterized enzymes and finding enzymes for target reactions remain major challenges. Despite recent advances in machine learning, translating enzyme function prediction into systematic discovery across the vast space of uncharacterized proteins and biochemical reactions remains challenging. Here we present EzHit, a lightweight framework for bidirectional enzyme reaction retrieval. Across enzyme annotation, orphan-reaction retrieval and family-specific fine-tuning benchmarks, EzHit achieved strong top-ranked performance and outperformed representative enzyme reaction matching baselines. We further show that Mahalanobis distance based geometric confidence provides more useful reliability estimates than probability-derived uncertainty metrics or evidential learning, enabling confidence-aware prioritization of high scoring candidates. Owing to its efficiency, EzHit was applied to a nearly trillion-scale OMG_Prot50 with RHEA screen, yielding 8.20 billion retained enzyme reaction associations across 30.27 million predicted enzyme sequences. Experimental validation further confirmed the activity of EzHit prioritized metagenomic enzyme candidates for a sparsely annotated reaction. Together, these results establish EzHit as a scalable framework for enzyme annotation, reaction-guided mining and biocatalyst discovery

Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.
desc: [Frontiers in artificial intelligence] Osteoporosis is a major global health burden, with considerable morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new avenues for osteoporosis screening, bone mineral density quantification, fracture-risk prediction, and clinical decision support, but progress remains fragmented across machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative models, and multimodal learning. This systematic review brings these strands together and identifies priority research needs for AI-based osteoporosis prediction. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, studies were identified from Scopus and Google Scholar, published between January 2020 and the final search date of 30 June 2026, with two reviewers screening independently and resolving disagreements by consensus. Design-related risk-of-bias indicators, such as retrospective vs. prospective design, validation strategy, and reference standard, were recorded for every study; a full PROBAST, QUADAS-2, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal is planned but not yet complete. Fifty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively and descriptively, without formal meta-analysis, given substantial heterogeneity. Findings spanned five themes: classical machine learning, deep learning for imaging, explainable AI, generative models, and multimodal learning. Deep learning achieved strong predictive accuracy (AUC 0.82-0.96), XAI improved clinical interpretability, generative models helped offset data scarcity, and multimodal approaches boosted performance by combining imaging and clinical data. Key gaps remain, including limited external validation, heavy reliance on retrospective data, poor generalisability, and limited regulatory readiness. Building on these findings, this review proposes MXGNet, a multimodal, explainable, generative framework incorporating privacy-preserving federated learning, intended to guide development of robust, interpretable, clinically deployable AI tools for osteoporosis prediction.

title: Case-Specific Priors-Guided Multimodal Fusion for Prognosis Prediction in Head and Neck Cancer
desc: Accurate prognosis prediction for head and neck cancer typically necessitates integrating highly heterogeneous clinical and pathological evidence by sophisticated multimodal fusion. However, existing fusion techniques are usually grounded in case-generic clinical rationales about complementary synergies across modalities, underestimating case-specific variance. In this study, we propose a prognosis prediction framework that explicitly incorporates Case-specific Priors to guide Multimodal fusion (named CPM). It leverages broad medical knowledge of LLMs to characterize each case's (case-specific) intra-modal contexts and inter-modal relations, as well as case-generic multimodal rationale, as priors, enabling three-stage priors-guided multimodal fusion: (i) Intra-modal Context-guided Calibration (IntraCC) that leverages case-specific intra-modal priors to guide feature calibration within each modality; (ii) Inter-modal Relation-guided Interaction (InterRI) that leverages case-specific inter-modal priors to guide pair-wise feature interaction in modality pairs; and (iii) Multimodal Rationale-guided Aggregation (MultiRA) that leverages case-generic multimodal priors to guide final feature aggregation over all modalities. On the well-established HANCOCK challenge dataset involving four distinct medical modalities, our CPM achieved a mean AUC of 83.98% for predicting 5-year overall survival and 2-year recurrence-free survival, improving upon the baseline by 7.58%, pioneeringly demonstrating the effectiveness of LLM-derived medical priors in guiding multimodal fusion for prognosis prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/yuelin421/CPM.

title: Kawasemi-Colours: an open end-to-end platform for structure-colour design based on avian structural colour
desc: Structural colour provides durable, pigment-free colouration by controlling the interaction of light with nanostructured materials rather than by using wavelength-selective pigments. In birds, non-iridescent blue and green plumage arises from coherent scattering by quasi-ordered keratin-air nanostructures, making these natural systems attractive models for sustainable colour engineering. Despite decades of research on their optical mechanisms, open end-to-end implementations that connect biological nanostructures with colour prediction, inverse design and physics-based evaluation remain limited. Here I present Kawasemi Colours, an open end-to-end platform for structure-colour design based on avian structural colour. From published electron micrographs, I assembled a provenance-tracked dataset of spongy, channel and quasi-ordered sphere nanostructures with associated colour metadata. I extracted interpretable structural descriptors, developed compact forward models that predict colour from nanostructure images, and implemented an analytic inverse design tool that generates candidate structures for a target colour. Both directions are provided through self-contained interactive web applications. Kawasemi Colours provides an open framework for studying and designing structural colour from biological nanostructures. By integrating curated data, interpretable machine learning, wave optics, and interactive design tools, the platform lowers the barrier to comparative structural-colour research and provides a cumulative foundation for testing and refining structure-colour relationships as new biological data become available.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma: A Modern Review of Pathogenesis and Treatment.
source: PubMed · The international journal of biochemistry & cell biology
desc: [The international journal of biochemistry & cell biology] Oral cancer (OC), predominantly oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), is a serious global health burden with high mortality rates, especially in South and Southeast Asia. OC is a severe worldwide health issue that is mostly caused by a sedentary lifestyle, alcohol, tobacco, and areca nut intake. The highest prevalence of OSCC is in India and Southeast Asia. Complex genomic and epigenetic changes, such as TP53 dysfunction, enhanced EGFR alteration, and dysregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathways, in conjunction with tumor-promoting alterations in the tumor microenvironment, contribute to oral carcinogenesis ( Tan et al., 2023). Oral submucous fibrosis (a chronic condition that causes precancerous progression in mouth), and leukoplakia (white or grey patches to form on mucus membrane) are instances of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), which are key indicators of cancer conversion. Even with advances in histopathology and imaging, delayed diagnosis remains a major limitation. Salivary biomarkers, liquid biopsy devices, and artificial intelligence-based screening tools are examples of novel diagnostic methods with potential for early diagnosis. Therapeutically, novel approaches such as immunotherapy, targeted therapy, nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, electro spun nanofibers, and plant-derived phytoformulations offer innovative, multi-targeted strategies with enhanced efficacy and reduce toxicity. However, surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy continue to be the primary treatment approaches. Improving new interventions for OC treatment needs a multifaceted approach that integrates early detection strategies, advanced therapeutic strategies, the use of plant-derived therapeutics, nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and public health awareness to get better therapeutic outcomes.

title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
desc: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network's head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.

Artificial intelligence in spatial transcriptomics: a review of methods, datasets, and directions.
desc: [Briefings in bioinformatics] Spatial transcriptomics (STs) measures gene expression while retaining the location of transcripts or cells within tissue sections. Unlike bulk RNA sequencing, which averages expression across cell populations, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which generally requires tissue dissociation, ST links molecular profiles to tissue architecture. This spatial information supports the analysis of tissue heterogeneity, cellular organization, and potential intercellular interactions. The spatially resolved nature of ST has unlocked diverse applications in fields such as cancer, neuroscience, reproductive biology, and plant biology. In parallel, the development of publicly accessible databases and repositories has facilitated large-scale, multi-cohort comparisons and benchmarking. The rapid expansion and increasing complexity of these datasets have driven the adoption of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. These computational tools support a range of tasks, including data pre-processing, image segmentation, spatial domain identification, and pattern recognition. Moreover, they are instrumental in integrative multi-omics analyses and predictive modeling. This AI-focused review provides necessary background on ST technologies and databases and evaluates the use of statistical, ML, and DL methods across the analytical workflow, from image and sequencing-data preprocessing to spatial analysis and LLM-assisted interpretation. We compile key resources related to datasets, AI-driven analytical frameworks, and ST data analysis pipelines, and discuss current challenges, limitations, and future directions for AI-based tools in spatial omics.

title: Data-Efficient Classifier Pretraining Through Diffusion Models
desc: Machine learning with limited data is susceptible to overfitting, especially with modern deep neural networks. Prior to the introduction of AlexNet, reconstruction-based pretraining with auto-encoder and denoising auto-encoder were found to be beneficial, partially due to the limited size of the training sets at the time. Motivated by these traditional approaches, we propose DiffPT, a simple diffusion modeling approach to pretrain a given classifier backbone for limited domain-specific training data. We experiment on time-series data, standard natural-image benchmarks, and medical imaging datasets, and contrast the diffusion approach to a multitude of modern and traditional un/self-supervised methods. While contrastive pretraining performs better on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet in low-data regimes, DiffPT is particularly effective on medical imaging and time-series tasks, where it outperforms self-supervised baselines across a range of low-data regimes. Our results suggest that DiffPT is a simple and effective approach for data-efficient classifier pretraining on different modalities.

AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings.
desc: [JMIR AI] Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets.
